q: The concept of ____ is very important for the physical and biological sciences.
e: Temperature indicates the energy changes in natural processes and is directly related to the energies of molecules composing an object.

q: This is because the ____ of an object is directly related to the energies of molecules composing the object.
e: The temperature of an object reflects the internal kinetic and potential energy of its constituent molecules.

q: Natural processes often involve energy changes and the ____ is an indicator for these changes.
e: Temperature serves as a measurable indicator of energy changes occurring during natural physical and biological processes.

q: It is expected that students will identify that thermal energy is an ____ of a matter.
e: Thermal energy is the total internal energy of matter, comprising both kinetic and potential energy of its molecules.

q: The sensations of hotness, warmness and coldness can be experienced by ____ objects.
e: Human senses can perceive relative hotness or coldness through direct physical contact with objects.

q: ____ is the quantity that determines how cold (or) how hot the object is.
e: Temperature is the physical quantity used to objectively measure the degree of hotness or coldness of a body.

q: To measure temperature accurately, we use instruments called ____.
e: Thermometers are specialized instruments designed to measure temperature accurately using thermometric properties.

q: The energy exchanged between an object and its surrounding due to different temperatures is defined as ____.
e: Heat is specifically defined as the energy in transit between systems or objects due to a temperature difference.

q: ____ is the energy in transit.
e: Heat is not stored energy; it is strictly the energy transferred or in transit between bodies at different temperatures.

q: The unit of heat is the same as units of ____.
e: Since heat is a form of energy transfer, it is measured in standard energy units such as Joules.

q: When a body at a higher temperature is in contact with a body at a lower temperature, ____ flows from the first to the second body.
e: The second law of thermodynamics dictates that heat naturally flows from a region of higher temperature to a region of lower temperature.

q: The motions and positions of molecules in matter result in the ____ energy and potential energy.
e: Molecular motion contributes to kinetic energy, while molecular positions and interactions contribute to potential energy.

q: The total energy, that is, the sum of the potential energy and the kinetic energy, of molecules in matter is in fact the ____ of that matter.
e: Internal energy is the comprehensive sum of all microscopic kinetic and potential energies within a substance.

q: Temperature is a measure of the ____ of molecules.
e: Temperature provides a macroscopic measure that is directly related to the average internal energy of the molecules in a substance.

q: Every thermometer uses a physical property that varies with ____.
e: Thermometers operate by measuring a physical property that changes predictably and continuously with temperature.

q: This property is referred to as the ____ property of the thermometer.
e: A thermometric property is any physical property that varies linearly and continuously with temperature, enabling temperature measurement.

q: For example, the thermometric property of a liquid-in-glass thermometer is the ____ of the liquid.
e: Liquid-in-glass thermometers rely on the predictable thermal expansion of the liquid inside the capillary tube as temperature changes.

q: The liquid-in-glass thermometer consists of a thin glass bulb joined to a ____ tube with a narrow bore which is sealed at its other end.
e: The capillary tube's narrow bore ensures that small changes in liquid volume result in visible changes in the liquid thread length.

q: When the bulb becomes warmer, the liquid in it expands more than the bulb so some of the liquid in the bulb is forced into the ____.
e: Differential expansion between the liquid and the glass forces the liquid up into the narrow capillary tube, indicating a temperature rise.

q: The thinner the bulb wall is, the ____ the response of the thermometer will be when the temperature changes.
e: A thinner bulb wall reduces thermal resistance, allowing heat to transfer more quickly and resulting in a faster thermometer response.

q: The liquid used usually contains ____ (or) coloured alcohol.
e: Mercury and coloured alcohol are the two most common liquids used in liquid-in-glass thermometers due to their distinct thermometric properties.

q: Alcohol has a lower ____ than mercury so it is more suitable for low-temperature measurements.
e: Alcohol remains liquid at much lower temperatures than mercury, making it ideal for measuring cold environments.

q: Thermocouple thermometers are electrical thermometers which make use of the ____ that develops when two different metals are in contact.
e: Thermocouples operate on the Seebeck effect, where a temperature difference between two dissimilar metal junctions generates a measurable voltage.

q: One of the junctions is maintained at ____ and the other junction is used as the temperature probe.
e: A reference junction is typically kept at a known constant temperature, such as 0℃, to calibrate the voltage reading of the probe junction.

q: Because of the small size of a thermocouple junction, thermocouple thermometers are used to measure ____ changing temperatures.
e: The low thermal mass of the small junction allows thermocouples to respond almost instantaneously to rapid temperature fluctuations.

q: In addition, they can be used to measure much ____ temperatures than liquid-in-glass thermometers.
e: Thermocouples can withstand and accurately measure extremely high temperatures that would melt or vaporize liquid-in-glass thermometers.

q: Resistance thermometer uses the fact that the electrical resistance of a metal (e.g platinum) wire ____ with temperature.
e: In a resistance thermometer, the electrical resistance of the metal wire increases predictably as the temperature rises.

q: A resistance thermometer can measure temperatures accurately in the range ____ to 1200℃ and best for steady temperatures, but it is bulky.
e: Resistance thermometers offer high accuracy over a wide range from -200℃ to 1200℃, though their bulkiness limits certain applications.

q: Thermometric substances can be ____, liquids (or) gases.
e: Thermometric properties can be observed and utilized in all three states of matter: solids, liquids, and gases.

q: They have physical properties that vary continuously and ____ with temperature.
e: For a substance to be a good thermometric material, its chosen physical property must vary both continuously and linearly with temperature.

q: Temperature units depend on the ____ used.
e: The numerical value and unit of a temperature measurement are determined by the specific temperature scale being applied.

q: The temperature scales most widely used today are Celsius (Centigrade), ____ and Kelvin scales.
e: Celsius, Fahrenheit, and Kelvin are the three primary temperature scales utilized in scientific and everyday contexts.

q: The SI unit of temperature is ____.
e: The Kelvin scale is the base unit of thermodynamic temperature in the International System of Units (SI).

q: To calibrate a thermometer, two ____ points are chosen and the interval between these points is subdivided into a number of equal parts.
e: Calibration requires two fixed, reproducible reference points to establish a reliable and standardized temperature scale.

q: The freezing point and boiling point of water under normal ____ pressure are chosen as reference points which are marked on the thermometer.
e: Standard atmospheric pressure is required to ensure the freezing and boiling points of water remain consistent and reproducible for calibration.

q: The interval between these two points is divided into ____ equal parts for the Celsius scale.
e: The Celsius scale is a centigrade scale, meaning the interval between the ice point and steam point is divided into 100 equal degrees.

q: If the freezing point of water (or) ice point is marked 0℃ and the boiling point of water (or) steam point is marked ____, the thermometer scale is the Celsius scale.
e: The defining fixed points of the Celsius scale are 0℃ for the freezing point of water and 100℃ for the boiling point of water.

q: On the Celsius scale, the ice point is ____ and the steam point is 100℃.
e: The ice point, or freezing point of water, is defined as exactly 0℃ on the Celsius temperature scale.

q: On the Fahrenheit scale the ice point is ____ and the steam point 212 F.
e: On the Fahrenheit scale, the freezing point of water (ice point) is set at 32°F, while the boiling point is 212°F.

q: On the Kelvin scale the ice point is ____ and the steam point is 373 K.
e: The Kelvin scale sets the ice point of water at 273 K, which corresponds to 0℃ on the Celsius scale.

q: For example, normal body temperature is ____ °F.
e: Normal human body temperature is widely recognized as 98.6°F, which is equivalent to 37.0℃.

q: The relationship between the Celsius temperature $T_c$ and kelvin temperature $T_K$ is given by ____.
e: To convert a temperature from Celsius to Kelvin, you add 273 to the Celsius value, as the Kelvin scale starts at absolute zero.

q: The lowest air temperature recorded in the world is ____.
e: The lowest naturally occurring air temperature ever recorded on Earth was 184 K, measured in Antarctica.

q: This temperature was measured in ____ in 1983.
e: The record low temperature of 184 K (-89℃) was documented in Antarctica, the coldest continent on Earth.

q: When a substance is heated, its ____ usually increases.
e: Heating a substance generally causes its molecules to move more vigorously, leading to an increase in the overall volume of the substance.

q: The ____ of the substance increase correspondingly.
e: As volume increases due to heating, the physical dimensions (length, area, or volume) of the substance expand correspondingly.

q: This increase in size can be explained in terms of the increased ____ energy of the molecules.
e: Thermal expansion is driven by the increased kinetic energy of molecules, causing them to vibrate more vigorously and occupy more space.

q: The additional kinetic energy results in each molecule colliding more ____ with its neighbours.
e: Higher kinetic energy causes molecules to collide more forcefully, pushing each other further apart and resulting in expansion.

q: Therefore, the molecules push each other further apart and the substance which is heated increases in ____.
e: The cumulative effect of molecules pushing further apart is a macroscopic increase in the overall size of the heated substance.

q: Increasing the temperature of a gas at constant ____ cause the volume of the gas to increase.
e: According to Charles's Law, the volume of a gas increases with temperature when the pressure is held constant.

q: This increase occurs not only for gases, but also for liquids and ____.
e: Thermal expansion is a universal phenomenon that affects gases, liquids, and solids, though the magnitude of expansion varies.

q: In general, if the temperature of a substance increases, so does its ____.
e: A fundamental principle of thermal physics is that an increase in temperature generally leads to an increase in the volume of a substance.

q: This phenomenon is known as ____.
e: Thermal expansion is the scientific term for the tendency of matter to change its shape, area, and volume in response to a change in temperature.

q: You may have noticed that the concrete roadway segments of a sidewalk are separated by ____.
e: Expansion joints or gaps are intentionally left in concrete structures to accommodate thermal expansion and prevent structural damage.

q: This is necessary because concrete expands with increasing ____.
e: Concrete, like most solids, undergoes thermal expansion when exposed to higher temperatures, requiring space to expand into.

q: Without these gaps, thermal expansion would cause the segments to push against each other, and they would eventually ____ and break apart.
e: If thermal expansion is constrained, the resulting compressive stress can cause the concrete segments to buckle and fracture.

q: Although two different metal bars of the same length are heated such that the increase in temperature is the same, the ____ of their expansion may not be the same.
e: Different materials have different coefficients of linear expansion, meaning they will expand by different magnitudes even under identical conditions.

q: For example, the expansion of copper is ____ times that of steel.
e: Copper has a higher coefficient of linear expansion than steel, causing it to expand one and a half times as much for the same temperature change.

q: ____ expands twice as much as steel does.
e: Aluminium has a significantly higher coefficient of linear expansion compared to steel, expanding twice as much under the same thermal conditions.

q: The dependence of the change in length of an object on its original length and change in temperature is ____.
e: This formula mathematically describes linear expansion, relating the change in length to the original length, temperature change, and the material's expansion coefficient.

q: In the formula $\Delta l = \alpha l \Delta T$, $\alpha$ represents the ____.
e: The symbol $\alpha$ denotes the coefficient of linear expansion, a material-specific constant that quantifies how much the material expands per degree of temperature change.

q: The coefficient of linear expansion is the change in length per ____ length for one degree change in temperature.
e: By definition, the coefficient of linear expansion measures the fractional change in length (change per unit length) for each degree of temperature change.

q: The unit of $\alpha$ is per K, which can be written as ____.
e: Since the coefficient of linear expansion represents a fractional change per degree, its SI unit is inverse Kelvin, written as $K^{-1}$.

q: The coefficient of linear expansion for steel is ____.
e: Steel has a relatively low coefficient of linear expansion, valued at $1.27 	imes 10^{-5} K^{-1}$, making it dimensionally stable under temperature changes.

q: Therefore, the length of the metal bar at $T + \Delta T$ is ____.
e: This equation calculates the final length of an object after thermal expansion by adding the change in length to the original length.

q: The relations analogous to the one which gives the increase in length $\Delta l$ for the increase in temperature $\Delta T$ can be derived for the area expansion and ____.
e: The principles of linear expansion can be extended to two dimensions for area expansion and three dimensions for volume expansion.

q: The relation obtained for area expansion is ____.
e: This formula calculates the change in area ($\Delta A$) based on the original area ($A$), the coefficient of area expansion ($ eta$), and the temperature change ($\Delta T$).

q: The relation obtained for volume expansion is ____.
e: This formula calculates the change in volume ($\Delta V$) based on the original volume ($V$), the coefficient of volume expansion ($\gamma$), and the temperature change ($\Delta T$).

q: In the equation $\Delta A =  eta A \Delta T$, $ eta$ is the ____.
e: The symbol $ eta$ represents the coefficient of area expansion, which quantifies the fractional change in area per degree of temperature change.

q: The coefficient of area expansion of a substance is the change in area per unit area for one ____ change in temperature.
e: The coefficient of area expansion is defined specifically as the change in area per unit area for each single degree of temperature change.

q: The coefficient of volume expansion of a substance is the change in volume per unit volume for one degree change in ____.
e: The coefficient of volume expansion measures the fractional change in volume for each degree of temperature change.

q: Generally all substances expand on heating and ____ on cooling.
e: The general rule of thermal physics is that substances expand when heated due to increased molecular motion, and contract when cooled.

q: But in the case of water the behavior is different, when water at 0℃ is heated its volume decreases up to ____ and density increases.
e: Water exhibits unique behavior between 0℃ and 4℃, where it contracts upon heating, leading to an increase in density.

q: At 4℃ the ____ becomes maximum and beyond this temperature volume start to increase.
e: Water reaches its maximum density at 4℃; above this temperature, it behaves normally and expands as it is heated further.

q: This unusual expansion of water is called ____ of water.
e: The anomalous expansion of water refers to its unique property of contracting when heated from 0℃ to 4℃, contrary to most other substances.
